entries.title: Problem-Based Software Requirements Specification
entries.publisher: Rafael Gorski M. Souza and Paulo Cézar Stadzisz, Revista Eletrônica de Sistemas de Informação
entries.why: Starts from named customer problems, not requested features, and derives customer needs and requirements from them. In an AI programme, every capability, including each agent, should then trace to a problem it solves.
entries.check: Confirm every requirement derives from a customer need, and each need from a named customer problem; cut the rest. MIT-licensed agent skill: github.com/RafaelGorski/Problem-Based-SRS.

entries.title: Rules of Machine Learning: Best Practices for ML Engineering
entries.why: Its first rule is not to be afraid to launch without machine learning. That sets the right opening question for any sponsor: what simple baseline must the AI beat to justify its cost?
entries.check: Ship a heuristic or non-ML baseline first, instrument it, and require every model to beat it on the same metric.

entries.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
entries.why: The ML code is a small fraction of a production ML system; the surrounding data, configuration and serving code carry most of the long-term cost. Budget for that, not for the demo.
entries.check: Inventory undeclared consumers, data dependencies and feedback loops around each model before committing to scale it.

entries.title: Building effective agents
entries.why: Separates predefined workflows from autonomous agents and argues for the simplest design that works. The publisher flags that the tooling described has since changed; read it for the design reasoning.
entries.check: For each proposed agent, document why a fixed workflow would not meet the requirement before granting it open-ended control.

entries.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
entries.why: Measures capability as the length of task, in skilled human time, that a model completes half the time. A sober way to set scope: delegate work inside that horizon, not beyond it.
entries.check: Estimate how long your target tasks take a skilled person and compare that with the published time horizon of the model you plan to use.

entries.title: "Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work": Data Cascades in High-Stakes AI
entries.publisher: Nithya Sambasivan et al., ACM CHI
entries.why: In interviews with 53 practitioners, 92% had met compounding data failures that surfaced late. The study ties them to practices that undervalue data work, which leaders can change.
entries.check: Log when each data issue was introduced and when it was detected; the gap is your cascade exposure.

entries.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
entries.why: Introduces pass^k: the chance an agent succeeds on every one of k repeated attempts at the same task. A pilot that passes once is a demo; consistency is what customers experience.
entries.check: Run each evaluation task several times and report pass^k alongside the single-run success rate.

entries.title: AI Agents That Matter
entries.why: Shows that agent evaluations often ignore cost and lack proper holdout sets, so headline accuracy can mislead. Ask for accuracy and cost together, measured on tasks the agent has not seen.
entries.check: Plot every candidate agent on cost versus accuracy, including simple baselines, and require results on a held-out task set.

entries.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
entries.why: Strong models can approximate human preference ratings, which makes evaluation at scale affordable. The paper also documents position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases that must be controlled before trusting the scores.
entries.check: Swap answer order, vary length and use a different model family as judge; report agreement with a human-labelled sample.

entries.title: Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation of LLM Outputs with Human Preferences
entries.why: Finds that people refine their evaluation criteria while grading outputs, so automated graders must be revisited as understanding grows. Evaluation is a managed asset, not a one-time setup.
entries.check: Version your grading criteria and LLM-judge prompts, and re-measure their agreement with human grades whenever criteria change.

entries.title: Underspecification Presents Challenges for Credibility in Modern Machine Learning
entries.why: Models with equally strong test scores can behave very differently in deployment. A strong pilot result does not, on its own, predict production behaviour.
entries.check: Evaluate candidate models on shifted and subgroup data that the pilot test set does not represent.

entries.title: Inspect
entries.publisher: UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs
entries.why: An open-source evaluation framework co-developed by the UK AI Security Institute, covering coding, agentic and reasoning tasks. A shared, inspectable harness makes results reproducible and comparable across model vendors.
entries.check: Express pilot evaluations as versioned Inspect tasks so the same suite reruns unchanged on every model or prompt change.

entries.title: Datasheets for Datasets
entries.publisher: Timnit Gebru et al., Communications of the ACM
entries.why: A standard set of questions about how a dataset was collected, labelled and intended to be used. Without those answers, no one can say whether pilot data represents production.
entries.check: Require a datasheet for every evaluation and fine-tuning dataset, including its collection process, known gaps and permitted uses.

entries.title: Reliable Product Launches at Scale
entries.why: Describes how Google turned launches into a repeatable discipline with a dedicated coordination role and a checklist. AI launches need the same rigour, plus questions specific to model behaviour.
entries.check: Extend the launch checklist with rows for evaluation results, abuse testing, rollback of model and prompt versions, and cost limits.

entries.title: Canarying Releases
entries.why: Expose a change to a small share of traffic, compare it against a control, then widen. For models and prompts, whose failures are statistical rather than crashes, this comparison is an essential safety net.
entries.check: Route model and prompt changes through a canary with a control group and predefined quality, latency and cost thresholds.

entries.title: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction
entries.publisher: Eric Breck et al., IEEE Big Data
entries.why: Twenty-eight specific tests and monitoring needs drawn from a wide range of production ML systems. It turns 'is this ready for production?' into a score a review board can track.
entries.check: Score each system against the rubric at launch review and treat untested sections as open risks with named owners.

entries.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
entries.why: The shared vocabulary security teams use for LLM application risk, from prompt injection to unbounded consumption. Asking which items a launch has mitigated is a fast, credible review question.
entries.check: Map each of the ten risks to a named control or an accepted-risk decision in the launch review record.

entries.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026
entries.why: A peer-reviewed list of the most critical security risks for autonomous and agentic AI systems. Use it alongside the LLM Top 10 once a system can act, not just answer.
entries.check: Verify each agent runs with its own scoped identity and least-privilege tool permissions, never a shared human or service account.

entries.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
entries.publisher: UK NCSC, US CISA and international partners
entries.why: Joint guidance from national cyber security agencies, organised by lifecycle: secure design, development, deployment, and operation and maintenance. A security baseline a board can point to.
entries.check: Confirm model weights, prompts and tool credentials are covered by the same asset inventory, access control and incident process as code.

entries.title: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
entries.why: A model update shipped on positive evaluations and A/B results despite expert testers saying it felt off, then was rolled back. OpenAI committed to treating behaviour issues as launch-blocking.
entries.check: Give named expert reviewers authority to block a model release on qualitative findings, even when quantitative evaluations pass.

entries.title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
entries.publisher: Saleema Amershi et al., Microsoft Research (ACM CHI)
entries.why: Eighteen guidelines, validated with 49 design practitioners, for how AI features set expectations, handle mistakes and support correction. They shape how users experience the system on the days it is wrong.
entries.check: Review the launch UI against the guidelines on efficient correction, efficient dismissal and explaining why the system did what it did.

entries.title: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations
entries.why: NIST's reference taxonomy of attacks on predictive and generative AI, including direct and indirect prompt injection and the security of agents. One vocabulary for security, engineering and risk teams.
entries.check: Use its attack categories as the headings of your AI threat model so findings map to a public reference.

entries.title: Model Context Protocol Specification (2026-07-28)
entries.why: An open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Standardising on one protocol reduces bespoke integration work and gives security teams a single interface to review.
entries.check: Pin the protocol revision your servers support and review its authorization section before exposing any MCP server beyond localhost.

entries.title: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification
entries.why: An open protocol for agents built by different teams or vendors to discover each other and delegate tasks. It matters once agents multiply and must cooperate across organisational boundaries.
entries.check: Treat each Agent Card as an interface contract: version it, sign it, and review its declared skills and security schemes.

entries.title: The Tail at Scale
entries.publisher: Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso, Communications of the ACM
entries.why: Brief latency spikes that are harmless in small systems come to dominate performance at scale. Agent workflows that chain many model and tool calls inherit this problem directly.
entries.check: Measure p99 latency per step and end to end for agent runs, and set per-call timeouts and hedging where steps are idempotent.

entries.title: Addressing Cascading Failures
entries.why: Explains how overload in one component spreads through retries and dependencies until a whole service fails. Agents that retry automatically can turn a model-provider slowdown into exactly this.
entries.check: Cap retries with budgets and jittered backoff, propagate deadlines through agent steps, and load-test the provider-throttled case.

entries.title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
entries.publisher: Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia and James Zou
entries.why: Routing each query through a cascade, cheaper models first and stronger ones only when needed, matched the best single model at up to 98% lower cost. Model choice is a per-request decision.
entries.check: Log which model served each request and at what cost, then test whether a cheaper first-pass model meets the quality bar.

entries.title: FinOps for AI Overview
entries.why: Vendor-neutral practice for allocating and controlling AI spend, including token-based pricing and scarce GPU capacity. AI costs move faster and reach more teams than typical cloud spend.
entries.check: Tag every model call with team, product and use case so cost per outcome can be reported, not just total spend.

entries.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
entries.why: A taxonomy of fourteen failure modes from expert-annotated traces, grouped into system design, misalignment between agents, and task verification. Adding agents adds coordination risk, not only capability.
entries.check: Classify failed multi-agent runs with the paper's taxonomy, and require an explicit verification step before any agent marks a task complete.

entries.title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
entries.why: Proposes agent designs with provable resistance to prompt injection by limiting what an agent can do after reading untrusted input. Each trades some utility for security, a choice the business should own.
entries.check: For each agent, identify where untrusted content enters and which pattern, such as plan-then-execute, constrains actions after that point.

entries.title: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
entries.why: Agents increasingly act on delegated credentials, and agent protocols such as MCP authorise through OAuth. This is the IETF's current security baseline for OAuth deployments.
entries.check: Confirm agent access tokens are audience-restricted and sender-constrained, and that public-client refresh tokens are rotated or sender-constrained.

entries.title: Semantic conventions for generative AI systems
entries.why: The open standard for recording model calls, agent steps, tool use and token usage as telemetry. It keeps observability portable across vendors. Still marked Development, so expect changes.
entries.check: Emit gen_ai spans and token-usage metrics for every model and tool call, and record which convention version each service emits.

entries.title: Trace Context
entries.why: The web standard for carrying a trace identifier across services. When one user request passes through several agents, tools and vendors, it is what lets you reconstruct the whole path.
entries.check: Confirm traceparent headers propagate through every agent hop, tool call and third-party API, including asynchronous queues.

entries.title: Service Level Objectives
entries.why: Defines reliability through indicators and objectives that reflect what users notice, and makes the target explicit. For AI systems, answer quality belongs beside latency and availability.
entries.check: Define at least one quality SLI per AI feature, such as graded answer acceptability on sampled traffic, with an explicit SLO target.

entries.title: Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure
entries.why: Blameless postmortems turn incidents into durable fixes and shared knowledge. AI incidents, such as harmful outputs or quality regressions, deserve the same written review as outages.
entries.check: Add AI-specific triggers to the postmortem policy: a quality regression, a harmful output reaching users, or an agent acting outside its scope.

entries.title: A postmortem of three recent issues
entries.why: Three infrastructure bugs intermittently degraded responses, and the evaluations in place did not capture what users were reporting. Quality can regress in production through infrastructure alone.
entries.check: Run quality evaluations continuously against true production endpoints, and keep a privacy-safe path to investigate user-reported bad outputs.

entries.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
entries.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
entries.why: EU law that tiers obligations by risk and places duties on deployers as well as providers. Obligations phase in over several years; establish which apply to your systems, and from when.
entries.check: Classify each AI system against Article 6 and Annex III, and confirm logging and human-oversight duties for any high-risk use.

entries.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system
entries.why: The certifiable management-system standard for AI, built on the same structure as ISO/IEC 27001. It gives boards an auditable answer to who owns AI risk, how it is assessed, and how it improves.
entries.check: Map existing AI controls to the standard's Annex A and record gaps before deciding whether to pursue certification.

entries.title: ISO/IEC 42005:2025 Information technology — Artificial intelligence (AI) — AI system impact assessment
entries.why: Guidance on assessing how an AI system may affect individuals and society, and when in the lifecycle to do it. Done early, it shapes scope; done late, it becomes paperwork.
entries.check: Run the impact assessment before build and again at each material change, and link results to the risk register.

entries.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
entries.why: A voluntary framework organised around four functions: govern, map, measure and manage. Useful as common language between risk, legal and engineering. NIST has announced it is being revised.
entries.check: Map each AI system's controls to the four functions and name an accountable owner for every gap.

entries.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
entries.why: Applies the AI RMF to generative AI, defining risks novel to or worsened by it, such as confabulation and value-chain integration, with suggested actions. A practical basis for governance reviews.
entries.check: Check the launch risk register covers each of the profile's risk categories, with an owner and a chosen action or explicit acceptance.

entries.title: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems
entries.why: Defines the parties in an agent's lifecycle and proposes initial practices such as constraining actions, requiring approval, attributability and interruptibility. A starting map of who is accountable when an agent acts.
entries.check: For each production agent, confirm actions are attributable to a principal and that a tested shutdown path exists.

entries.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
entries.why: A short, standard record of what a model is for, how it was evaluated, and where it should not be used. Write one before launch, not after an incident.
entries.check: Maintain a card for each deployed model or agent, including disaggregated evaluation results and explicitly out-of-scope uses.

entries.title: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
entries.publisher: Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia
entries.why: A tribunal held an airline liable for its website chatbot's incorrect advice, rejecting the idea that the chatbot was responsible for its own actions. A small claim, but a clear signal.
entries.check: Ensure customer-facing AI answers on policy, price or entitlement are grounded in the authoritative source and logged for later review.

entries.title: Ironies of automation
entries.why: Automation erodes the skills and attention people need to supervise it and take over when it fails. Every 'human in the loop' promise for agents has to be designed against this.
entries.check: For each human approval step, measure approval rates and review time; near-total approval with seconds of review signals rubber-stamping.
